# The Opus 5 Prove-It Kit

Claude Opus 5 launched on 2026-07-24 with the model ID `claude-opus-5`. It is already the default model on Claude Max and the strongest model available on Claude Pro. Your team is running it on client work right now, whether or not anyone tested it first.

This kit is how you find out where it is genuinely ready for your work and where it still needs a human on top.

This is not a benchmark. A benchmark scores a model on tasks you will never run. This is a structured self-test you run on your own five hardest recurring tasks, so the answer is about your client work and nobody else's. You manufacture the receipt instead of trusting the launch post.

## Why now

The honest clock: the model shipped today and it is already the default on Max, so the untested assumption is already live in your workflow. The value of testing is highest before you quietly rewire how your team works around a model nobody checked. Ten minutes of structured testing today beats finding the gap inside a client deliverable next month.

## What is in here

```
README.md                  <- you are here
prove-it/SKILL.md          the harness that runs the whole test for you
eval-rubric.md             what a score of 1, 3, or 5 actually means
task-slots.md              your five real tasks (you fill this in)
verdict-report.md          the output: scores, a verdict, and what it cost
CLAUDE-PROJECT-SETUP.md    how to load this into Claude Code or a claude.ai Project
```

## Build order

1. Load the kit. Open `CLAUDE-PROJECT-SETUP.md` and follow the path for your setup (Claude Code or a claude.ai Project). Five minutes, no code.
2. Fill `task-slots.md`. Replace the five example tasks with your five hardest recurring ones and attach real context for each. This is the only file you edit by hand.
3. Invoke the skill. Tell Claude to run the Prove-It harness. It interviews you if any slot is thin, then runs each task twice at two effort settings and scores every output against the rubric.
4. Read `verdict-report.md`. Each task comes back with a deploy / keep-a-human / retest verdict and the real token cost of finding out.

## The 30-minute run plan

- 0:00 to 0:05  Load the kit (CLAUDE-PROJECT-SETUP.md)
- 0:05 to 0:15  Fill your five task slots with real context
- 0:15 to 0:27  Run the skill: two passes per task, scored
- 0:27 to 0:30  Read the verdict and the cost line

If your context is already sitting in a folder or a doc, the fill step is faster and you finish under 30.

## What you need to know about Opus 5 before you start

These are the only launch facts this kit relies on:

- Launched 2026-07-24, model ID `claude-opus-5`.
- The fourth model in the Claude 5 family in under two months, after Mythos 5, Fable 5, and Sonnet 5 in June.
- Anthropic says it comes close to the frontier intelligence of Claude Fable 5 at half the price.
- Pricing is 5 dollars per million input tokens and 25 dollars per million output tokens, unchanged from Opus 4.8.
- It is the default model on Claude Max and the strongest on Claude Pro.
- It has an adjustable effort setting that trades intelligence against speed and token cost. This kit runs every task at two effort settings on purpose, because the question that matters is whether it holds up at the effort level you would actually pay for. Effort changes the answer, so you test both.
- There is a fast mode at roughly 2x the price for about 2.5x the speed.

No benchmark numbers, no invented percentages. The only numbers in your report are the ones your own runs produce.

## The one rule that matters

Run your hardest task first. If Opus 5 holds up on the worst one at the effort you would actually use, the easy tasks take care of themselves. If it breaks there, you found the ceiling before a client did.

Want the harder version of this pointed at your whole agency? Book a free fit call: https://calendly.com/ivan-intelligents/30min

Ivan Manfredi

---
name: prove-it
description: Run the Opus 5 Prove-It harness. Collects the founder's five hardest recurring tasks, runs each one twice at two effort settings on Claude Opus 5, scores every output against eval-rubric.md, and fills verdict-report.md with a deploy / keep-a-human / retest decision plus the real token cost. Use when the user says "run the prove-it kit", "test Opus 5 on my work", or "prove it".
---

# Prove-It: the Opus 5 self-test harness

You are running a structured self-test for an agency founder. The goal is a defensible, per-task answer to one question: on THIS founder's real recurring work, where is Claude Opus 5 ready to run with light review, and where does it still need a human on top?

This is not a benchmark. You are not comparing Opus 5 to other models or to public scores. You score its output on the founder's own tasks against a fixed rubric, at two effort settings, so the answer is specific to their client work.

Read `eval-rubric.md` before you score anything. Read `task-slots.md` for the founder's tasks. Write results into a copy of `verdict-report.md`.

## Protocol

### Step 0 - Orient (say this)

"I'm going to run the Opus 5 Prove-It test on five of your hardest recurring tasks. For each one I'll produce the output twice, once at high effort and once at low effort, then score both against a fixed rubric and give you a deploy / keep-a-human / retest verdict. First let me check your task slots."

Open `task-slots.md`. For each of the five slots, check it has (a) a clear task instruction and (b) real attached context: a brief, a transcript, last month's numbers, the actual client email.

### Step 1 - Interview for anything thin

For any slot missing real context, ask, one at a time, in these words:

- "Task {n} says '{task title}'. Paste the real input this task normally starts from: the brief, the email thread, the data, whatever you'd actually hand a team member. I won't invent it."
- "What does a genuinely good output for task {n} look like to you? One sentence on what 'client-ready' means here."
- "At what effort setting would you actually run this in real life if it worked: high (slower, pricier, maximum reasoning) or low (fast, cheap)? Your deploy decision hangs on that setting."

Do not proceed to Step 2 for a task until it has real context. A test on invented input proves nothing. If the founder cannot supply real context for a slot, mark it SKIPPED in the report and move on.

### Step 2 - Run each task twice, at two effort settings

For each task, produce the deliverable TWICE using Claude Opus 5:

- Pass A, high effort. Maximum reasoning. On Claude Max or Pro, turn extended thinking on, or set the effort control to its highest setting. On the API, set the effort setting to high on the request. This is the slowest, most expensive, most capable pass.
- Pass B, low effort. On Claude Max or Pro, turn extended thinking off, or set the effort control to its lowest, fastest setting. On the API, set the effort setting to low. This is the fast, cheap pass.

If your interface labels the control differently, the two passes are simply one at maximum reasoning and one at fast and economical. Run the same task, same context, same instruction, both times. Do not improve the input between passes.

For each pass, record the input token count and output token count reported by your interface. You need them for the cost line.

Produce the actual deliverable each time. Do not summarize what you would write. Write it.

### Step 3 - Score every output against the rubric

For each pass (A and B) of each task, open `eval-rubric.md` and score all four criteria (correctness, judgment, format adherence, tone/client-readiness) on the 1 to 5 scale, using the written anchors. For each criterion, write one concrete sentence citing the specific line or choice in the output that earned the score. No score without a reason pointing at the text.

Be a tough editor. A 5 means you would send it to the client as-is. A 3 means a competent draft with real gaps. Default to the lower anchor when torn.

### Step 4 - Fill the verdict report

Open `verdict-report.md` and fill it in for all five tasks. For each task record:

- the four scores at Pass A and at Pass B
- the effort setting the founder said they'd actually run (from Step 1)
- the verdict at THAT setting, using the decision rules in verdict-report.md
- the token counts for both passes

Then compute the cost line using only the founder's recorded token counts and the published Opus 5 prices: 5 dollars per million input tokens, 25 dollars per million output tokens. Show the arithmetic.

End with the one-paragraph readout: which tasks Opus 5 can take off the founder's plate today at the effort they'd run, which to keep a human on, and which to retest after they improve the context.

## Rules

- Never invent input. Real context, or the task is SKIPPED.
- Never score without citing the specific text that earned it.
- Never soften a score to be encouraging. The founder is about to trust this on client work.
- Never report a benchmark number or a comparison to another model. Only the founder's own runs and the published prices.
- If Pass A and Pass B score the same on a task, say so plainly. That is a real and useful result: the expensive setting bought nothing for that task, so run it cheap.

files.name: eval-rubric.md
files.description: What a score of 1, 3, or 5 actually means, with two worked examples of scoring real agency output.
files.content:
# The Prove-It scoring rubric

Four criteria. Each scored 1, 3, or 5 using the written anchors below. Score the 2s and 4s as "between these two." Every score cites the specific line that earned it, or it does not count.

The rubric exists so "good" means the same thing on Monday and Thursday, on task one and task five. Without fixed anchors, a self-test drifts into "seems fine," which is how untested models end up inside client deliverables.

## Criterion 1 - Correctness

Are the facts, numbers, names, and logic right?

- 1: Contains a claim that is wrong, a number that does not add up, a fabricated fact, or a made-up detail about the client. Would embarrass you if sent.
- 3: Broadly right, with a soft spot: a figure you'd want to double-check, a claim stated more confidently than the input supports, or a small logical gap.
- 5: Every factual claim traces to the input you gave it. Numbers reconcile. Nothing invented. You could stand behind every line in front of the client.

## Criterion 2 - Judgment

Did it make the calls a good operator would make: what to include, what to cut, what to flag, what to prioritize?

- 1: Dumps everything at one level, misses the obvious priority, or gives advice that would hurt the client. No sense of what matters.
- 3: Reasonable calls, but generic. Covers the bases without picking the one thing that actually moves this client's situation.
- 5: Leads with what matters most for this specific client, cuts the noise, and flags the real risk or tradeoff a senior person would raise unprompted.

## Criterion 3 - Format adherence

Did it follow the structure, length, and constraints you asked for?

- 1: Ignored the format. Wrong length, wrong structure, added sections you didn't ask for, or buried the deliverable under preamble.
- 3: Mostly followed it, with drift: slightly too long, one section off-brief, or a stray "here is your..." wrapper you'd delete.
- 5: Exactly the shape you asked for. Right length, right sections, no filler, drops straight into your deliverable with no reformatting.

## Criterion 4 - Tone and client-readiness

Would this go to a paying client as-is, in your voice?

- 1: Off-voice, hedged, robotic, or full of the tells (delve, leverage, seamless, "in today's landscape"). You'd rewrite it from scratch.
- 3: Professional and clean, but generic. Reads like a competent stranger wrote it rather than you or your firm. You'd rework the opening and the close.
- 5: Sounds like your firm on a good day. You could paste it into the email or the doc and send it with a light read, no rewrite.

## Worked example A - a proposal section

Task: "Write the 'Scope' section of a proposal for a 12-person B2B agency, from the attached discovery-call notes. Under 200 words. Our voice: plain, specific, no fluff."

Output (excerpt):

> "In today's fast-paced digital landscape, we will leverage a holistic approach to unlock your agency's full potential. Our robust methodology delivers seamless results across all touchpoints. Deliverables include: strategy, execution, and optimization."

Scoring:

- Correctness 3: nothing is factually wrong, but "strategy, execution, and optimization" is not traceable to the discovery notes, which named lead routing and reporting specifically. It generalized past the real input.
- Judgment 1: it ignored the two concrete problems from the call (lead routing, reporting) and wrote a horoscope that would fit any agency. A good operator leads with the client's named pain.
- Format adherence 3: under 200 words and has a scope shape, but the three-word deliverable list is thinner than a proposal needs.
- Tone and client-readiness 1: "fast-paced digital landscape," "leverage," "holistic," "unlock," "robust," "seamless" are the exact tells the brief said to avoid. Full rewrite.

Read: fails on your work. Keep-a-human, or retest with the discovery notes actually pasted in and a stricter voice instruction.

## Worked example B - a client diagnosis

Task: "From the attached 3 months of funnel numbers, tell this e-commerce client where their drop-off is and what to fix first. Two paragraphs, direct."

Output (excerpt):

> "Traffic held steady at ~18k sessions/mo. Add-to-cart is healthy at 9%, but checkout completion fell from 71% to 52% over the three months, concentrated after the May checkout redesign. That single step is costing roughly 340 orders/mo at your stated AOV. Fix the checkout regression before spending another dollar on traffic. Everything upstream is working."

Scoring:

- Correctness 5: every number traces to the attached data, the 71 to 52 drop and the ~340 orders are arithmetic you can re-run, and it located the break at checkout correctly.
- Judgment 5: it set aside the steady-traffic vanity metric, found the one step that broke, tied it to a real event (the May redesign), and gave a clear first move with a reason to hold traffic spend.
- Format adherence 5: two paragraphs, direct, no preamble.
- Tone and client-readiness 5: reads like a sharp operator talking straight. Sendable with a light read.

Read: deploy on this task, and if Pass B (low effort) scores the same, run it cheap.

## How to use the scores

The scores feed `verdict-report.md`. The short version: a task is "deploy" only when it clears the bar on correctness AND client-readiness at the effort level you would actually run it. Everything else stays human-in-the-loop, for now.

files.name: task-slots.md
files.description: Your five hardest recurring tasks. Replace the examples with real work and attach real context.
files.content:
# Your five task slots

Replace each example below with a real recurring task from your own agency, and attach the real context it starts from. The whole test is only as honest as what you put here. Invented tasks give you a benchmark of nothing.

Pick your FIVE hardest recurring tasks: the ones that eat senior time, the ones where a bad output reaches a client, the ones you keep meaning to hand off but never trust to. Those are where knowing the answer is worth the most.

For each slot, fill:

- Task: what you're asking for, exactly as you'd brief a team member.
- Context: paste or attach the real input (brief, transcript, numbers, thread). Do not describe it. Attach it.
- Format: the shape, length, and constraints of a good output.
- Deploy effort: the effort setting you'd actually run this at in real life (high or low). Your verdict hangs on this.

---

## Slot 1 - Proposal draft  [EXAMPLE, replace me]

- Task: Draft the scope and pricing-rationale section of a proposal from discovery-call notes.
- Context: [paste the real discovery-call notes or transcript here]
- Format: Two sections, under 300 words total, our house voice, no filler.
- Deploy effort: high

## Slot 2 - Client funnel diagnosis  [EXAMPLE, replace me]

- Task: From the client's last 90 days of funnel data, find the biggest drop-off and name the first fix.
- Context: [paste the real numbers or attach the export here]
- Format: Two short paragraphs, direct, one clear first move with a reason.
- Deploy effort: high

## Slot 3 - Positioning call  [EXAMPLE, replace me]

- Task: A prospect is torn between two positioning angles. Recommend one and say why, in their market.
- Context: [paste the prospect's site copy, market notes, and the two angles here]
- Format: A recommendation, three reasons, one risk to watch. Under 250 words.
- Deploy effort: high

## Slot 4 - Scope-creep reply  [EXAMPLE, replace me]

- Task: A client is asking for work outside the agreed scope. Write a reply that holds the line and keeps the relationship warm.
- Context: [paste the client's real message and the original scope here]
- Format: A short email in our voice. Firm, friendly, no defensiveness.
- Deploy effort: low

## Slot 5 - Monthly report narrative  [EXAMPLE, replace me]

- Task: Turn this month's numbers into the narrative section of the client report: what happened, what it means, what we're doing next.
- Context: [paste this month's metrics and last month's for comparison here]
- Format: Three short paragraphs, plain language a busy founder reads in one pass.
- Deploy effort: low

---

When all five slots hold a real task with real context attached, tell Claude to run the Prove-It harness (see prove-it/SKILL.md). It will interview you for anything still thin, then run and score each one.

# Verdict report - Opus 5 on my own work

Filled by the Prove-It harness. One block per task, both effort settings, a verdict at the setting you'd actually run, and the real cost of running this test.

- Model tested: claude-opus-5
- Date run: [fill]
- Effort settings compared: high (maximum reasoning) vs low (fast, cheap)

## Per-task scores

Each criterion scored 1 to 5 (see eval-rubric.md). Pass A = high effort, Pass B = low effort.

### Task 1 - [title]

| Criterion | Pass A (high) | Pass B (low) |
|---|---|---|
| Correctness | _ | _ |
| Judgment | _ | _ |
| Format adherence | _ | _ |
| Tone / client-readiness | _ | _ |

- Deploy effort you'd actually run: [high / low]
- Score at that effort: correctness _ , client-readiness _
- One line on where it broke or held: [___]
- Tokens: Pass A in/out _ / _ , Pass B in/out _ / _
- VERDICT: [DEPLOY / KEEP-A-HUMAN / RETEST]

### Task 2 - [title]

(repeat the block above)

### Task 3 - [title]

(repeat the block above)

### Task 4 - [title]

(repeat the block above)

### Task 5 - [title]

(repeat the block above)

## Decision rules

Apply these at the effort setting you said you'd actually run the task, scoring that pass rather than your best pass:

- DEPLOY: correctness >= 4 AND tone/client-readiness >= 4, with no single criterion at 1. Opus 5 can take this task off your plate with a light review. Set up the review step and move on.
- KEEP-A-HUMAN: any criterion at 1, OR correctness or client-readiness at 3 or below. It writes a useful draft and a person still has to finish it before it reaches a client. Fine. Now you know the draft is worth starting from.
- RETEST: the scores were low but the input was thin, vague, or missing context. Improve `task-slots.md` for that task and run it again before you judge the model. Do not blame the model for a bad brief.

Effort note: if Pass B (low effort) scores the same as Pass A (high effort) on a task, run that task at low effort. High effort was buying reasoning that changed nothing. If high effort clears the bar and low effort does not, the task is a DEPLOY only at high effort, and your cost line should reflect that you'll run it there.

## What this cost to find out

Computed only from the token counts recorded above and the published Opus 5 prices: 5 dollars per million input tokens, 25 dollars per million output tokens.

```
input cost  = (total input tokens  / 1,000,000) * $5
output cost = (total output tokens / 1,000,000) * $25
test cost   = input cost + output cost
```

- Total input tokens across all passes: _
- Total output tokens across all passes: _
- Input cost: $_
- Output cost: $_
- Total cost of this test: $_

That is the whole price of knowing, before you wire an untested model into client work. For context, fast mode runs about 2.5x faster at roughly 2x the token price, so a task you mark DEPLOY at low effort can be run faster for more, if speed is worth it to you.

## The readout

In one paragraph: which tasks Opus 5 can run today at the effort you'd actually use, which stay human-in-the-loop for now, and which to retest once the input is better. Write it plainly, the way you'd tell a partner what you found.

files.content:
# Load the kit into Claude - two paths

Pick the one that matches how you use Claude. Both take about five minutes. No coding either way.

## Which one am I?

- You have Claude Code (the app that works inside a folder on your computer): Path A.
- You use Claude in the browser at claude.ai on a Max or Pro plan: Path B.

Either works. Path B is the one most non-developers want.

## Path A - Claude Code

1. Put this whole `opus-5-prove-it-kit` folder somewhere on your machine.
2. Open Claude Code in that folder, or point it at the folder.
3. Confirm Opus 5 is the active model. On Claude Max it is the default, so you likely don't have to change anything.
4. Type: `Run the Prove-It harness in prove-it/SKILL.md on my task-slots.md.`
5. Claude reads the skill and the rubric, interviews you for anything thin in your task slots, runs each task twice, scores them, and writes your `verdict-report.md`.

That's it. The skill file drives the whole run.

## Path B - a claude.ai Project (browser, Max or Pro)

1. Go to claude.ai and create a new Project. Call it "Opus 5 Prove-It."
2. Confirm the Project uses Opus 5. On Max it is the default model; on Pro it is the strongest option, so select it.
3. Add the kit files to the Project's knowledge: upload `prove-it/SKILL.md`, `eval-rubric.md`, `task-slots.md`, and `verdict-report.md`. You can drag them in.
4. Fill your five real tasks into `task-slots.md` first, then upload that version, so the Project has your actual work to test.
5. Open a chat in the Project and paste this kickoff line:

   "You have a skill file (prove-it/SKILL.md), a rubric (eval-rubric.md), my five tasks (task-slots.md), and a report template (verdict-report.md) in your knowledge. Follow prove-it/SKILL.md exactly: interview me for anything thin, run each of my tasks twice at high and low effort, score every output against the rubric, and give me the filled verdict report. Start now."

6. Answer its interview questions with real context, and let it run.

## Setting the two effort levels (both paths)

The test runs each task twice, once at high effort and once at low.

- In the browser or Claude Code: turn extended thinking ON for the high-effort pass and OFF for the low-effort pass, or set the effort control to its highest and lowest settings if your interface shows one.
- On the API: set the effort setting to high on one request and low on the other.

If the labels differ in your interface, the two passes are simply one at maximum reasoning and one at fast and economical. Claude will tell you which pass it is on.

## If you get stuck

Tell Claude: "You're running the Prove-It kit. Re-read prove-it/SKILL.md and tell me the exact next step." The skill is written to get you back on rails.
